claims.text: Stepwise thermo-mechanical processing can induce multiple coherent precipitate phases in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The induced coherent precipitate phases can produce an ultrahigh-strength, ductile refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed strategy produces lower density than the as-cast or homogenized counterpart.
The initial refractory HEA is a random solid solution.
A balanced mixture of heavy refractory elements such as W and Ta and lighter refractory elements such as Ti and V reduces overall alloy density.
Hot rolling followed by cold rolling, annealing, aging, and quenching is an applicable stepwise processing sequence.
Annealing and aging temperatures are around 900 °C.
Water quenching can be used after aging to retain the processed microstructure.
The treatment forms δ-lamellae followed by γ″ particles.
The δ-lamellae have dimensions of tens of nanometers.
The precipitates are dispersed in a refined BCC matrix.
Coherent precipitates strengthen the alloy by acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
Dislocations can shear the coherent precipitates, preserving ductility while increasing strength.
Grain-size refinement contributes to a reduction in density.
The treatment can increase yield or ultimate tensile strength by approximately 1–2 GPa relative to untreated material.
The treated alloy maintains or improves ductility relative to untreated material.
The treated alloy has lower weight than a similar alloy without light-element inclusion and microstructural tailoring.
The as-cast alloy has lower strength than the stepwise-processed alloy.
The as-cast or conventionally processed alloy has lower ductility and higher density because its heavy refractory elements are uniformly distributed.
Excessive treatment can generate undesirable brittle phases, and scaling from small samples to bulk components can limit the benefits.

contradictions.description: The predicted density benefit is defined relative to an alloy without light-element inclusion, but the proposed experiment compares samples with identical nominal compositions, so it cannot test the effect of light-element inclusion.

The mechanism attributes density reduction primarily to alloy composition, while the falsification rule demands a density reduction between identically composed samples that differ only in thermo-mechanical processing.
The conditions place both annealing and aging around 900 °C, whereas the cited stepwise treatment uses annealing at 900 °C but aging at 650 °C.
